3. Data and sample selection

Our analyses require each firm-quarter observation to include an earnings press release,
the MD&A section of the 10-Q or 10-K filing and financial variables. We begin with the
23,017 quarterly earnings press releases analyzed in Davis et al. 2011. These press releases
were published by PR Newswire between January 1, 1998 and December 31, 2003 and
were identified as related to earnings announcements by PR Newswire. <sup>13</sup> Next, we obtain
the Forms 10-K or 10-Q corresponding to the earnings press release for each firm quarter
using 10-K Wizard (now Morningstar Document Research) and extract the MD&A
portion of each filing. <sup>14</sup> For annual reports, we capture the portion of the filing beginning
with ‘‘Section 7’’ or ‘‘Management’s Discussion’’ (or variations) and ending with ‘‘Section
8.’’ Many firms incorporate Section 7A ‘‘Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about
Market Risk’’ into Section 7 instead of as a stand-alone item. To be consistent across the
sample, we include Section 7A in the MD&A for all our observations. For quarterly
reports we follow a similar process using slightly different search strings because the
MD&A in the 10-Q is in section 2.

While SEC filings are fairly standardized, the grammar, layout, and word choice across
filings differ in some cases. Therefore, our search strings are unable to exactly identify and
extract the MD&A for every filing. To examine the extent of this problem we review a random sample of 150 SEC filings and the MD&A extracted from them. We find our process

11. It is also possible that the verifiability of managers’ statements differs across the earnings press release and
the MD&A for reasons unrelated to managers’ strategic reporting incentives, which could affect our language measures if verifiability is associated with managers’ use of pessimistic or optimistic language. However, we are not overly concerned that verifiability is an omitted correlated variable as we have no reason
to expect that our proxies for the intensity of managers’ strategic reporting incentives would be correlated
with the verifiability of managers’ statements.
12. In an examination of the asymmetric market response to good versus bad news, Kothari, Shu, and
Wysocki (2009) find that managers, on average, delay the release of bad news to investors. Kothari et al.
argue that managers accumulate bad news until it reaches a threshold level (i.e., the costs of withholding
the bad news exceed the benefits), at which point they voluntarily disclose it. While their findings are consistent with strategic disclosure, it is important to note that firms are required to issue an earnings press
release and MD&A, whereas Kothari et al. examine strictly voluntary disclosures (i.e., dividend changes
and management forecasts). Thus, we address the question, given that firms have to provide some narrative discussion of performance for a given quarter, how do managers that have negative or pessimistic
news to report choose to disclose it across the alternative outlets?
13. Davis et al. (2011) eliminated observations for which certain accounting and financial market variables
required in their study were not available on COMPUSTAT, Center for Research in Security Prices, or
I ⁄ B ⁄ E ⁄ S.Given the similarity in the nature of variables used in this study relative to Davis et al., we
expect that starting with the population of earnings press releases published by PR Newswire during this
sample period would yield a very similar sample.
14. Li (2008) uses 10-K and 10-Q filings directly from EDGAR. However, we found many text files from
EDGAR include a large number of extraneous characters, likely due to the firm and EDGAR using different text-file formats. 10-K Wizard runs EDGAR text files through an algorithm to reformat the files and
produce a ‘‘clean’’ text file which is amenable to computerized search tools.

We retain 16,923 press release observations for which we have a matching MD&A and
the financial variables necessary to complete our tests. In addition to missing financial variables, there are four reasons we lose observations. First, there are some press release observations for which there is not a matching 10-Q or 10-K filing available on 10-K Wizard. Second,
we eliminate observations for firms filing as small businesses because the format of their filings differs from standard filers and because small business filers likely differ systematically
from standard filers along other important dimensions. Third, we exclude all observations for
which the MD&A is less than 200 words, which generally occurs when our extraction process
does not capture the MD&A or when the filing describes the MD&A as ‘‘incorporated by reference’’. Fourth, we eliminate late filers, which are firms filing the 10-K more than 90 days
after the quarter end, or filing the 10-Q more than 45 days after quarter end.

Measures used to quantify language


We employ textual analysis software, DICTION 5.0, to measure managers’ use of pessimistic and optimistic language in their narrative disclosures. DICTION 5.0 (Hart 2000,
2001) has been used extensively to analyze narrative discourse in other fields and more
recently to analyze earnings press releases (e.g., Davis et al. 2011; Demers and Vega 2010).
DICTION is a dictionary-based program that counts types of words most frequently
encountered in contemporary American public discourse and is designed to capture the
linguistic style (i.e., verbal tone) of narratives (Hart 1984). DICTION uses 10,000 search
words assigned to 35 theoretically based linguistic categories to characterize text on several
dimensions (Pennebaker, Mehl, and Niederhoffer 2003). We use DICTION to quantify
managers’ use of pessimistic and optimistic language in their earnings press releases and
the MD&A included in their 10-K and 10-Q filings. <sup>16</sup>

For each earnings press release, we define the variables PESS_PR and OPT_PR
as the percentage of words in the text that are pessimistic or optimistic, respectively. Likewise, for each MD&A disclosure, we define the variables PESS_MDA and OPT_MDA as
the percentage of words in the text that are pessimistic or optimistic, respectively. <sup>17</sup>

Numerical characters are excluded from all calculations
